actions.name: Visual inspection of right foot wound via camera
actions.result: Dressing soaked through with greenish-yellow drainage with foul odor. Periwound erythema extends from forefoot across mid-foot to approximately 2 cm below the ankle, margin not sharply demarcated. Surgical site at great toe has partially separated edges. No visible bone or black necrotic tissue.

actions.name: Current temperature (home thermometer)
actions.result: 38.1 C (100.6 F) oral, reported by patient

actions.name: Measure extent of erythema (patient marks border with pen, measures with tape)
actions.result: Erythema border now 11 cm proximal to original surgical margin, measured by patient self-marking with pen and tape via camera guidance; was 4 cm at discharge per clinician measurement from wound margin using photo documentation (home log photo). Note: the two measurements were taken by different observers using different techniques, so the comparison should be treated as an approximate trend rather than a precise, directly comparable measurement.

actions.name: Monofilament/light touch sensation check, bilateral feet (patient self-test with cotton ball per instruction)
actions.result: Patient reports markedly reduced sensation to light touch on both feet, worse at the toes, with difficulty feeling the cotton ball at the distal aspects bilaterally.

actions.name: Capillary refill, toes bilaterally (camera-guided)
actions.result: Right great toe refill 4 seconds (delayed); other toes and left foot refill under 2 seconds

actions.name: Review hospital discharge summary
actions.result: Discharged after 6 days IV antibiotics and surgical debridement for right first-toe diabetic foot infection with surrounding cellulitis; osteomyelitis not evident on plain films at that time (plain films have limited sensitivity and do not definitively exclude bone infection). Cultures grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) and group B Streptococcus; discharged on amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID x14 days, new insulin glargine 14 units subcutaneous nightly, home dressing changes BID with wife as caregiver, follow-up in clinic in 9 days.

actions.name: Review home glucose log
actions.result: Readings over past 2 days range 260-340 mg/dL; no readings below 150 mg/dL recorded.

actions.name: Review current medication list
actions.result: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID, insulin glargine 14 units SC nightly, metformin 1000 mg PO BID (home medication, continued), lisinopril 10 mg PO daily (home medication, continued).

actions.name: Ask patient to demonstrate insulin pen technique on camera
actions.result: Patient dials pen to 14 units correctly but hesitates on injection site rotation and is unsure whether air bubble must be cleared each time; does not prime the pen before the demonstrated dose.

actions.name: Foot and lower-leg skin survey, bilateral, via camera
actions.result: Right foot: described erythema/edema as above. Left foot: skin intact, no ulceration, mild dryness, no erythema. Both feet: distal pulses not directly visualized by camera; patient reports no numbness changes other than longstanding neuropathy.

actions.name: Pain assessment (0-10 scale)
actions.result: Right foot pain rated 3/10 at rest, patient notes this is similar to or less than pain at discharge despite worsening appearance; attributes to 'numbness.'

actions.name: Mental status and orientation check
actions.result: Alert and oriented x4, answers appropriately, no acute confusion.

actions.name: Review footwear and offloading instructions from discharge
actions.result: Discharge instructions specify non-weight-bearing/offloading of right foot with wound boot provided; patient instructed to avoid prolonged standing or walking.

actions.name: Review antibiotic adherence against pharmacy refill/dosing record
actions.result: Pharmacy fill record shows a 14-day supply of amoxicillin-clavulanate dispensed at discharge with no early refill requested; pill count/dosing pattern consistent with twice-daily use, no gaps identified in the dispensing record.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Worsening right foot surgical/diabetic infection with signs of ascending cellulitis and possible systemic sepsis response (fever, tachycardia, spreading erythema, purulent drainage) in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes two days after hospital discharge.
differential: Progressing cellulitis/surgical site infection without systemic sepsis
Early sepsis secondary to diabetic foot infection
Deep vein thrombosis of the leg (less likely, no calf swelling/pain described)
Contact dermatitis or dressing irritation (does not explain fever/drainage)
keyFindings: Spreading erythema (approximately 4 cm at discharge, clinician-measured from wound margin via photo, to approximately 11 cm now, patient self-marked and tape-measured) with foul-smelling greenish drainage; note the two measurements used different observers and techniques, so the magnitude of change should be interpreted as an approximate trend, not an exact comparison
Subjective fever 38.1C and tachycardia 102 bpm with chills overnight
Delayed capillary refill in the affected toe
Hyperglycemia 260-340 mg/dL with inconsistent insulin administration
Patient has been weight-bearing on the foot against offloading instructions
Pain reported as mild due to underlying neuropathy, which may mask severity of worsening infection
Insulin pen technique has gaps (no priming, uncertain site rotation) contributing to erratic glucose control
plan: Escalate immediately to the discharging provider/surgical team via SBAR: new fever, tachycardia, markedly increased erythema, purulent malodorous drainage, and hyperglycemia in a patient 2 days post-op for diabetic foot infection with known MSSA/group B Streptococcus culture — recommend urgent in-person evaluation today, not wait for the 9-day follow-up

Do not independently diagnose sepsis or change antibiotic/insulin orders; this is outside RN scope — communicate findings and let the provider determine disposition (ED vs urgent clinic vs home health escalation)

Reinforce strict non-weight-bearing/offloading of the right foot until seen; discuss safe alternatives for getting to the corral (cane, wheelchair, asking spouse/family for help, deferring non-essential tasks)
Provide focused teaching on insulin pen priming and injection site rotation; arrange follow-up teaching or home health nursing visit if available
Educate on glucose log reporting and the importance of taking insulin at the prescribed time (nightly) rather than variable administration

Document objective wound measurements, photos if system allows, and vital signs trend to support the SBAR handoff, noting that discharge and current erythema measurements were taken by different observers using different techniques and should be framed as a trend rather than a precise delta
Arrange transportation given 70-mile distance from hospital; ask about resources (family, community health transport) to get to care today
Advise patient and wife on signs of worsening sepsis to seek emergency care immediately (confusion, worsening fever, rapid heart rate, inability to keep fluids down) while awaiting provider callback
redFlags: Fever and tachycardia in a post-surgical diabetic foot infection patient
Markedly increased erythema extent over 2 days (clinician-measured 4 cm at discharge vs. patient self-measured 11 cm now, measured differently but still concerning for rapid spread)
Purulent, foul-smelling drainage suggesting uncontrolled or recurrent infection
Delayed capillary refill in the affected digit
Persistent hyperglycemia with inconsistent insulin dosing increasing infection risk and impairing healing
Continued weight-bearing on an infected, neuropathic foot risking further tissue damage
educationPoints: Diabetic foot infections can worsen quickly after discharge; new fever, spreading redness, or increasing drainage are urgent, not wait-and-see, findings
Peripheral neuropathy can blunt pain perception, so pain level alone should not be used to judge how serious a foot infection is
Insulin pens must be primed before each use to ensure accurate dosing, and injection sites should be rotated to avoid lipohypertrophy and absorption problems
Consistent nightly basal insulin dosing is important for glucose control and wound healing; skipping or shifting timing increases risk of hyperglycemia
Offloading (not walking on the healing foot) is as important as antibiotics and dressing changes for wound healing
Patients living in rural/remote areas need an explicit, realistic transportation plan built into any urgent referral

When comparing wound measurements over time, note whether the same observer and technique were used; mixing clinician-measured and patient self-measured values introduces imprecision and should be acknowledged when reporting trends

artifacts.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
artifacts.author: Dr. A. Benally, General Surgery
artifacts.body: 68-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus admitted for right first-toe diabetic foot infection with surrounding cellulitis. Underwent surgical debridement of right great toe. Wound cultures grew methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus and group B Streptococcus, both susceptible to the discharge antibiotic. Plain films at admission did not show osteomyelitis; given the known low sensitivity of plain radiographs for early bone infection, this does not definitively rule it out. Treated with 6 days IV ampicillin-sulbactam, transitioned to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID to complete a 14-day course. Started on insulin glargine 14 units SC nightly for persistently elevated inpatient glucose (metformin to be continued). Discharged home with wife performing BID dressing changes using provided supplies. Wound boot provided; patient instructed on strict non-weight-bearing/offloading of right foot. Follow-up in surgical clinic in 9 days or sooner if concerns. At discharge, erythema margin marked and measured at 4 cm from incision edge, photo on file.

cells: New diagnosis diabetes management, started this admission

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient says the foot 'looks about the same' as when he left hospital.
mismatches.recordEvidence: The discharge wound note records mild erythema about 4 cm from the wound margin with a dry, intact dressing and no purulent drainage. Today the dressing is soaked with foul-smelling greenish drainage and the redness reaches the mid-foot and beyond.
mismatches.teachingPoint: A stoic patient with neuropathy may sincerely report no change. Compare what you see with the documented baseline rather than relying on the patient's summary, and name the difference to him plainly and without blame.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports taking insulin glargine in the morning on some days and skipping it twice, rather than nightly as prescribed.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list and discharge summary specify insulin glargine 14 units subcutaneous nightly; the home glucose log shows persistently elevated readings 260-340 mg/dL consistent with the reported inconsistent/mistimed dosing.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Mismatched insulin timing and missed doses directly explain the hyperglycemia seen in the glucose log; reconciling the medication list against actual patient behavior is essential to identify correctable causes of poor glucose control, especially during active infection when glycemic control affects healing.

objectives.text: Recognize signs of worsening infection and possible systemic sepsis response in a post-surgical diabetic foot patient and escalate urgently via SBAR rather than deferring to the scheduled follow-up.
Identify barriers to insulin adherence (timing errors, missed doses, pen technique gaps) and provide appropriate patient education within RN scope.
Correlate hyperglycemia with insulin administration errors and infection severity, using the home glucose log and medication list.
Assess for diabetic peripheral neuropathy and its effect on symptom reporting (reduced pain despite worsening infection) and reinforce offloading/foot protection education.
Elicit psychosocial and logistical barriers (distance, transportation, reluctance to return to hospital) that affect the escalation plan, and problem-solve around them.
Identify a mismatch between patient-reported medication adherence and objective record evidence, and respond by exploring further rather than taking the history at face value.

patient.name: Raymond Tso
patient.appearance: An older man with a weathered, sun-worn face and short gray hair, wearing a plain flannel shirt. He is seated in a modestly furnished living room with wood paneling, leaning forward slightly with his right foot propped on a stool wrapped in a bulky dressing. His expression is calm but tired, and he pauses to think before answering each question.

persona.personality: Quiet, thoughtful, stoic; does not volunteer complaints readily and tends to downplay symptoms.
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks slowly and deliberately, pauses before answering, gives brief factual answers unless gently drawn out further.
persona.emotionalState: Calm on the surface but privately worried about returning to the hospital and burdening his wife or finances.
persona.background: Worked thirty-some years operating heavy equipment for a regional construction company before retiring to a small property with his wife, where they keep a few horses. They live about seventy miles from the nearest hospital in a rural part of northern Arizona. His wife has taken on most of the caregiving tasks since his surgery.
speechExamples: It looks about the same to me, I guess.
I don't want to make a big fuss over nothing.
My wife handles the bandage, she'd know better than me what it looks like.
I figured I'd just wait for the appointment in nine days.
I don't want to go back in there again so soon if I can help it.
concerns: Having to return to the hospital so soon after just getting home
The cost and logistics of another hospital visit, including the long drive
Being a burden to his wife who is already doing a lot of the caregiving
Whether the horses and ranch chores will get done if he can't do them

scenario.studentBrief: You are the home health/telehealth RN conducting a scheduled post-discharge follow-up call with Raymond Tso, 68, who was discharged 2 days ago after surgical debridement and IV antibiotics for a right great toe diabetic foot infection. He was started on new insulin glargine at discharge. Your task is to assess his wound, vital signs, glucose control, and medication adherence, and determine whether this can wait for his scheduled follow-up in 9 days or needs urgent escalation.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Post-discharge follow-up after diabetic foot infection with surgical debridement; patient reports foot 'looks about the same.'
scenario.openingLine: Hello, yes, this is Raymond. I guess you're calling about my foot. It looks about the same to me, nothing too different.
tasks: Perform a focused remote assessment of the surgical wound, vital signs, and glucose control
Take a medication history and review adherence to the discharge plan
Assess safety risks related to weight-bearing and foot care
Determine urgency and formulate an SBAR escalation to the provider if indicated
Provide patient-centered education on wound care and insulin administration

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in a rural property in northern Arizona, approximately 70 miles from the hospital.
profile.summary: A 68-year-old man two days post-discharge from surgical debridement and IV antibiotics for a diabetic foot infection presents for a routine telehealth nursing follow-up but shows new fever, tachycardia, spreading wound erythema, and purulent drainage alongside poorly controlled glucose and inconsistent insulin administration. The case trains learners to recognize escalating infection risk despite a stoic patient's minimization, reconcile medication adherence claims against objective evidence, and formulate an urgent SBAR handoff while addressing real rural logistical barriers to care.
profile.title: Post-Discharge Nursing Follow-Up: Worsening Diabetic Foot Infection After Debridement
